web_evidence.title: “Power and all its secrets”: Engendering Magic in Neil Gaiman’s The Ocean at the End of the Lane
web_evidence.note: Scholarly structural analysis identifies an unnamed first-person narrator in the frame and explains that the central childhood narrative follows the same narrator as a child.

web_evidence.title: The Ocean at the End of a Lane — Our Mythical Childhood Survey

web_evidence.title: “The Ocean at the End of the Lane”: Neil Gaiman returns
web_evidence.note: A contemporary review states that most action is recounted in first person and that the same unnamed narrator appears as an adult in the opening and closing frame.

person_note: The event quotes repeatedly expose an unnamed participating narrator recalling his own childhood as “I.” The sustained opening extract independently confirms first-person narration in the adult frame, while two scholarly structural sources establish that the central childhood recollection and closing frame belong to that same first-person narrator. Dialogue, universal maxims, and the isolated “she” description are local or nondiagnostic rather than contrary person shifts. The opening excerpt alone has limited scope, but the whole-book analyses resolve that limitation; no credible evidence of sustained second- or third-person sections was found.
